<reason>Side A won every major clash by exposing a fatal contradiction at the heart of Side B's case. Side B claimed both that social media users instantly recognize sponsored content and that requiring explicit verbal disclosures would ruin the "authenticity" of livestreams and short videos. Side A used its pressure questions and rebuttals to trap Side B on this point, eventually forcing Side B to admit in Rebuttal 2 that general skepticism does not tell viewers which specific product is paid and that explicit disclosure alters the "perceived unmediated relationship." Side A also cleanly dismantled Side B's feasibility and regulatory-arbitrage objections by pointing to integrated morning-show segments and the basic economics of sponsorship reach.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pressure question [A3.1] and follow-up in [A4.5]-[A4.7] & [A5.1]-[A5.2], which exposed that if stating "paid ad" aloud ruins an influencer's "authenticity," then that authenticity depends on deceiving viewers into thinking a paid pitch is an unmediated personal recommendation.</best_rebuttal>
